newsitem.title: CHINA: China brewing giant sees profits topping target.
newsitem.headline: China brewing giant sees profits topping target.

text.p: China's biggest brewer sees its profits ahead of target this year as it races to expand production to keep pace with growing demand for beer.
Beijing Yanjing Brewery Co Ltd, one of China's most successful state enterprises, is also in the unusual position of not seeking foreign help to boost its profits.
"We will do better than our target of 0.48 yuan per share for the full year and our first half profit will top 0.24 yuan," Ding Guangxue, deputy general manager, told Reuters.
"We don't really have a reason to seek a foreign partner," he said in an interview, speaking at the company's modern facilities on the outskirts of Beijing.

Yanjing Brewery expects more than 180 million yuan ($21.7 million) in pre-tax profits for the full year compared with 135 million last year. It plans to report its results for the first half next week.

Yanjing, with assets of 1.4 billion yuan, has a stranglehold on the capital's beer market with a commanding 85 percent share. Its total beer output has eclipsed even the better known Tsingtao Brewery.
Yanjing is 74.2 percent owned by the state, largely through the Beijing city government's hugely successful "red chip" company, Hong Kong-listed Beijing Enterprises.

Beijing Enterprises, which was nearly 1,300 times oversubscribed and saw its share price rocket on listing, holds 54 percent of Yanjing while the brewer has a 6.9 percent stake in the corporate parent.

While most brewers across China struggle to push output to efficient levels, Yanjing has added over 100,000 tonnes of production capacity each year over the last two years after adding 50,000 tonnes in each of the five years before that.
It added to its muscle by buying out rival Huasi Brewery last year, and now expects capacity of more than 700,000 tonnes this year against 580,000 tonnes in 1996.
Capacity should reach one million tonnes by the year 2000.
Last month, the brewery listed 72 million A shares for domestic investors on the nation's southern bourse of Shenzhen and that offer raised a total of 580 million yuan.
"Proceeds will be used to expand production and we expect to have most of that invested by the end of this year," Ding said.
The company has also a foothold in the nearby industrial city of Tianjin and surrounding Hebei province.
Ding attributes the success to producing the right-tasting -- some say sufficiently light-tasting beer -- for the local market.
"We have the taste that people in Beijing prefer," he said.

Yanjing was also one of the earliest brewers to go around the state distribution system and line up its own sales agents and it also had help from its designation as a key state enterprise, meaning that it had access to government funds even when credit was tight.
"We had to pay market rates but at least we got credit," Ding said.
Now, getting credit is no problem since the financially strong company is courted by the nation's banks.
Asked whether big foreign competitors crowding the domestic market were a threat to this big market share, Ding said the company was not worried.
"We are confident in our product."
Foreign brewers had approached the company, proposing cooperative deals, but Yanjing has been reluctant to give up a substantial share of its equity or promote another brand.
"We don't need their funds, since we have government support," Ding said. "We also have our own brand and a good market."
